analysis.one_liner: Lets courts and state attorneys general block weak or politically favorable antitrust settlements and case dismissals.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate with 9 Democratic sponsors, then referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it has had no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the rules for how the federal government settles antitrust cases. Courts would have to find that a proposed settlement (a 'consent decree') does not allow conduct that risks violating the antitrust laws, and merging companies would have to keep their assets separate while the court reviews the deal. Federal agencies would have to publish any plan to drop an antitrust case for 45 days first, and state attorneys general could take over the case if they object. The bill also requires disclosure of contacts between companies and government officials — including the White House — and of any benefits a company offered the government while its case was pending.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and workers affected by monopolized markets, small businesses competing against large merged firms, and state attorneys general who want a check on federal settlements or case dismissals they think are too soft.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, workers, small businesses, state attorneys general

how_it_helps.text: Courts must find that an antitrust settlement does not permit any transaction or business practice that creates a 'material risk' of violating the antitrust laws, and that the remedy is reasonably tailored to the alleged violations; the court need not defer to the government's predictions about whether its remedy will work.

In merger cases, the merging parties must keep the transaction's assets separate until 15 days after the agency responds to public comments, and a court can extend that freeze if the settlement looks unlikely to pass muster.

Any proposal to voluntarily dismiss an antitrust case brought by the Justice Department or FTC must be published at least 45 days in advance, the case is stayed during that window, and any state attorney general can move to substitute itself as plaintiff and take over the litigation with the government's case files.

The bill expands required disclosure of communications between companies and government officials — explicitly including the Executive Office of the President — and requires disclosure of any benefit or concession a party offered the government, including payments, donations, or policy changes the court finds reasonably connected to the proceeding.
State attorneys general can ask for an evidentiary hearing on a proposed settlement and, if one is held, are allowed to intervene in the case.

analysis.who_pays: Large companies facing antitrust cases: settlements would face harder judicial review, merger deals would sit in a longer asset-freeze period, and firms would face mandated disclosure of their contacts with White House and agency officials during litigation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Companies negotiating antitrust settlements with the government

drawbacks.text: The bill actually shortens the public comment window on proposed settlements from 60 days to 45 days, slightly reducing the time outside groups have to weigh in.

By making settlements harder for courts to approve and letting judges re-examine remedy choices, the bill could push agencies away from negotiated settlements toward years-long litigation, which delays relief for the markets those cases target.

Requiring asset freezes and extended disclosure of corporate-government communications adds legal uncertainty and cost for companies involved in mergers and antitrust cases, costs that could be passed along in deal timelines and legal spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core trade is a modest slowdown and added cost in antitrust cases for a much harder look at deals the government agrees to. The dismissals provision is the most concrete safeguard: today the Justice Department can drop an antitrust case with essentially no notice, and this bill would force 45 days of public exposure and let state attorneys general pick the case up. The shorter comment period is an odd fit for a bill titled for transparency, and critics could fairly argue the judicial-review standard handcuffs agency discretion. On balance the public-interest provisions outweigh the procedural friction, and the costs fall mainly on the companies being scrutinized.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 17, 2026 and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which has taken no further action on the record so far.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced S. 4107, the Antitrust Accountability and Transparency Act, on March 17, 2026, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee; the full action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote since referral.
All nine sponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one: the bill has only been referred to committee, and companies hoping for lenient antitrust settlements are unaffected while it sits.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits in committee

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored; the bill sits in a Senate Judiciary Committee controlled by Republicans, and no vote has occurred on the record.

industries.industry: Large corporations under antitrust scrutiny (major tech, telecom, and consolidation-prone sectors)
industries.note: Settlements would face real judicial review instead of near-automatic approval, merger deals would be frozen longer, and politically friendly case dismissals would become publicly visible and contestable. These firms' interests in quick, quiet settlements run against consumers and workers affected by concentrated markets.

industries.industry: Antitrust defense bar and corporate law firms
industries.note: More hearings, longer asset-freeze periods, and litigation instead of settlements mean more billable work but also more uncertainty for clients. The added complexity raises costs that companies weigh against settlement value.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors and the bill sitting in a Republican-controlled Senate Judiciary Committee with no scheduled action, the most likely path is that it receives no hearing or vote before the Congress ends on January 3, 2027, as most non-unanimous Senate bills referred to committee do.
